title: The yogis on the mountain
hookLine: Himalayan yogis ask why he stays in the world; he answers that you live in it without being stained

cards: On a bad day, the cabin fantasy goes like this. Quit everything. Move to a cabin in the mountains.
No inbox, no traffic, no difficult relatives, just silence and snow. In Nanak's time, some people really did it.
High in the Himalayas lived the sidhs, yogis who had left the world behind for caves and peaks, and who were said to have mastered the body and the mind.
On his journey north, tradition says, Nanak climbed up to meet them.

teach.b: Sidh means one who has succeeded, someone who has reached the goal, a perfected one. These yogis wore earrings and ash and carried begging bowls, and believed that to find the truth you had to leave ordinary life.
Bhai Gurdas tells a version of the meeting in his verses. The yogis ask how things are going down in the world.

teach.h: WHO LIGHTS THE WORLD, IF YOU HIDE?
teach.b: And Nanak answers, sharply, that the world is in darkness, because the people who should be lighting it have gone off to hide in the mountains.

There's also a long conversation with the yogis in the scripture itself, the Sidh Gosht, the talk with the sidhs, in raga Ramkali. They ask question after question, and one answer is the heart of this day.
How do you live in the world?

teach.h: LIKE A LOTUS, LIKE A DUCK.
teach.b: Like a lotus, he says, which grows in the water but floats clean on top. Like a duck, which swims in the stream and comes out dry. You don't have to leave the water.
You just don't let it soak in. That's the Sikh ideal in one picture, and it goes right back to Nanak.
Not the monk, not the hermit, but the householder: someone who works, raises a family, pays the bills, and keeps God in mind the whole time, unstained by greed and ego.
Sikhs don't look down on the yogis' devotion; Nanak spoke with them at length.
But his answer was a different path.

how: Sikhs follow the householder's path Guru Nanak taught, working and raising families rather than renouncing the world; the Sidh Gosht, his dialogue with the yogis, is part of the Guru Granth Sahib and is studied and sung.

o: a merchant who trades along the river
a perfected one who has reached the goal
a beggar who wanders from town to town

games.q: what's inside the meeting — tap the pairs.
p: swims in the stream, comes out dry
the talk with the sidhs, in Ramkali

s: Nanak told his followers to leave home for the mountains
he taught the householder's path: stay in the world, unstained.
a conversation with the yogis is in the Sikh scripture
the Sidh Gosht, in raga Ramkali.
Nanak refused to speak with the yogis
he talked with them at length, and answered their questions.

games.q: you're Nanak, high in the mountains. the yogis ask why you, a holy man, keep going back to your family and the world below. what do you answer?
o: you're right; I'll stay up here.
live in the world like a lotus in water.
the world is fine; there's nothing to worry about.
games.why: in the Sidh Gosht, he answers with the lotus that floats clean on the water, and the duck that swims and stays dry.

practice: Choose one ordinary chore, the dishes, folding laundry, wiping a counter, and if you can, begin it now, slowly. Feel the water, the cloth, the weight of the plate, and let your mind stay with your hands.
This is the lotus: right in the middle of ordinary life, and clean.

wordCard.voice: Sidh. A perfected one, the name for the yogis Nanak met in the mountains, who asked why he stayed in the world. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sidh, from Sanskrit siddha, one who has succeeded, a perfected yogi.

carryVoice: Your line: in the world, unstained. Tomorrow, a story with no twinkle in it. Day thirty-nine, done.
